To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a distributed population of neurons, each with a complex, eye-centered receptive field and an efferent copy of eye position, is capable of transforming visual inputs into eye orientation-dependent motor commands.

a 3-layer network trained to generate 3-D sccades developed distributed population motor fields with complex eye-centered receptive fields, widely-distributed fixed-vector motor commands and "gain field" eye-position sensitivity that rotated the population motor field into the correct visuomotor correspondence.

the oculomotor visuomotor system can be modeled as a 3-D visuomotor transform between a 2-D topographic map of visual receptive fields and a 6-D push-pull neural integrator, that the visuomtor transform is performed by a distributed population mechanism, and that the mechanism for this distributed population transform is the same one found in the real brain.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain uses a distributed population mechanism to transform the visual coordinates of visual receptive fields in the superior colliculi into the motor coordinates of the eye muscles.
the brain performs visuomotor coordinate transformations by a distributed, population mechanism, and that the network we have developed here is the first to demonstrate this.
the brain solves visuomotor coordinate transformations by using a population of neural units that are distributed over a 3-D reference frame.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain can solve complex, nonlinear, eye orientation dependent visuomotor problems with a simple and distributed mechanism.

distributed population mechanisms, such as those used by neural nets, can provide a powerful, parsimonious solution for the visuotopic-to-motor reference frame transformations required by the oculomotor control system.
the brain solves the visuomotot reference frame transformation problem by a distributed population mechanism, rather than a single unit mechanism, such as a "gain-field" neuron.
